Sup A: lopezmeza_2016 · Using simple models to describe the kinetics of growth, glucose consumption, and monoclonal antibody formation in naive and infliximab producer CHO cells
The model describes growth, glucose use, and infliximab-biosimilar production by native and recombinant CHO-S cells. It combines first-order growth during the exponential phase with a threshold-modified Monod growth relationship, a cell-yield description of glucose consumption, and a Luedeking–Piret description of antibody formation. The authors developed it using batch cultures in shake flasks at different initial glucose concentrations and temperatures, then evaluated its product-formation description in instrumented batch and fed-batch bioreactors. Cell, glucose, lactate, and active antibody concentrations were measured daily. The authors present the simple kinetic models as tools for understanding and characterizing cell-culture processes, and for applications such as monitoring, control, and optimization.
availability: The paper does not report a code or data repository.
cell lines: The model concerns native CHO-S cells and an in-house engineered recombinant CHO-S clone producing an infliximab biosimilar.
data processing: Cell and glucose profiles during exponential growth were fitted with second-order polynomials and differentiated to estimate growth and glucose-consumption rates.
data processing: For antibody-production analysis, viable-cell profiles were fitted with a sixth-order polynomial and differentiated to estimate cell-growth rates.
equipment: Instrumented bioreactor experiments used 1.6-L vessels with a 1.0-L working volume and were conducted only with recombinant cells.
equipment: Shake-flask batch cultures used 125-mL flasks with a 30-mL working volume.
estimation: For 37 °C recombinant batch data, the authors iteratively adjusted selected growth, yield, and production parameters while holding the threshold and one production coefficient fixed.
estimation: The authors selected the product-formation coefficients by fitting multiple cell-density and antibody-production data sets and numerically integrating the model.
estimation: The growth-kinetic parameters were obtained using Lineweaver–Burk linearization, and a linear regression was accepted only when its r² exceeded 0.97.
feeding: Shake-flask batch experiments tested initial glucose concentrations of 1.2, 2.4, 3.6, and 4.8 g/L.
feeding: The methods describe fed-batch operation with five intermittent additions of feed, each 10% of the initial culture volume, starting on day 1, and a temperature reduction on day 7.
fit: The authors report that the product-formation parameters fitted shake-flask data over initial substrate concentrations from 2.4 to 4.5 g/L.
growth: The authors treat cell growth as first-order in cell concentration during at least the initial portion of exponential growth.
growth: The fitted Monod parameters for recombinant cells were reported to change little with temperature, whereas those for naive cells changed with temperature.
growth: The growth relationship is Monod-type but includes a nonzero glucose threshold below which growth is not observed.
lactate: Lactate was measured and discussed, but the model laws described in the paper do not include a lactate balance or lactate effect.
limitations: A single pair of product-formation coefficients did not describe all the 37 °C batch data sets, and the authors suggest lactate inhibition as a possible model improvement.
measurement: Cell density and viability were measured by trypan-blue exclusion using a Guava easyCyte flow cytometer.
measurement: Glucose and lactate were measured by HPLC with refractive-index detection using an Aminex HPX 87H column and 5 mM sulfuric acid mobile phase.
measurement: The antibody assay quantified active monoclonal antibody in culture samples by ELISA.
measurement: The measured time series included viable cell density, glucose, lactic acid, and monoclonal antibody concentrations.
medium: Cultures used CD Opti CHO medium supplemented with 8 mM glutamine.
model size: The paper does not give a consolidated count of model states, equations, or estimated parameters.
model type: The authors characterize their approach as simple, unstructured kinetic modeling.
operation: Bioreactor batch runs lasted 10 days and fed-batch runs lasted 20 days, with duplicate cultures and daily sampling.
operation: Bioreactor cultures were agitated at 80 rpm and supplied with 2 standard L/h of gas to maintain dissolved oxygen at 40% saturation.
operation: Shake-flask cultures were inoculated at about 2 × 10⁵ viable cells/mL and incubated at 33 or 37 °C, 125 rpm, and 8% CO₂.
prior models: The authors contrast their approach with earlier recombinant-cell studies using structured kinetic, logistic, Monte Carlo, and regression models, including Sandadi et al. 2011, Goudar et al. 2009, Xing et al. 2010, and Farges et al. 2008.
prior models: The paper places its growth model alongside Monod-like and logistic hybridoma models, Monod and metabolic-flux models, and dynamic metabolic models for nonproducing CHO cells.
prior models: The product-formation model is identified as a Luedeking–Piret model, citing Luedeking and Piret 1959.
product: Antibody formation is represented with a Luedeking–Piret model, combining growth-associated and viable-cell-associated production.
product: The authors describe production by this recombinant line as mixed-mode, with formation related to both growth rate and viable-cell concentration.
sampling: Shake-flask cultures were run in triplicate with daily sampling and were stopped after 7 days for recombinant cells or 10 days for naive cells.
scope: The authors state that the proposed product-formation parameters fit experimental data sets in the range of 31–33 °C.
substrate use: The authors found that the cell/substrate yield coefficient varied with glucose concentration rather than remaining constant.
substrate use: The model relates glucose consumption to cell growth through a cell/substrate yield coefficient.
use: The authors propose simple kinetic models as practical tools for process characterization, online monitoring, process control, and optimization.
validation: For fed-batch validation, the paper describes a representative instrumented run with a temperature shift from 37 to 33 °C on day 7.
validation: The authors also applied the batch-derived kinetic parameter set to fed-batch cultures, where they report that the model fit the measured data.
validation: The product-formation description was tested on recombinant-cell batch cultures in instrumented bioreactors, and the authors report a good fit using the shake-flask parameter set.

Sup B: osberghaus_2012_rapid_equilibrium_sma · Determination of parameters for the steric mass action model—A comparison between two approaches (Rapid-equilibrium SMA)
The rapid-equilibrium steric mass action model represents protein binding and elution during strong cation-exchange chromatography. It predicts protein retention and outlet chromatograms by combining column transport, particle mass transfer, and SMA sorption, which represents competition between salt ions and proteins for binding capacity as well as protein shielding of binding sites. The paper compares estimating SMA parameters from gradient and breakthrough experiments with estimating them by inverse fitting of a mechanistic column model. Experiments used ribonuclease A, cytochrome c, and lysozyme on a prepacked 1 ml SP Sepharose FF column at pH 5 and pH 7. The authors use the comparison and noise analysis to assess parameter reliability and prediction, and recommend inverse fitting for process development because it predicts complete chromatograms.
availability: The paper identifies Matlab and Unicorn software used in the work but does not report a public code or data repository.
calibration: Approach I obtains the steric factor from breakthrough data after determining characteristic charge and equilibrium coefficient from gradient data.
calibration: External bed parameters were characterized using pulse and displacement experiments, with each experiment repeated at least three times.
calibration: Packed-bed and transport inputs for the inverse model included ionic capacity, axial dispersion, interstitial velocity, porosities, film transfer, and column and particle geometry.
calibration: The first approach derived SMA parameters from gradient retention data and frontal breakthrough data using the procedure of Brooks and Cramer (1992) and Shukla et al. (1998).
calibration: The inverse approach estimated SMA parameters by least-squares fitting of the mechanistic model to chromatograms, using Matlab's lsqnonlin procedure.
calibration: The lumped film-transfer coefficient was estimated by inverse fitting the mechanistic model to tracer peaks from pulse experiments.
comparison: The authors report comparable high predictivity from both parameter-estimation approaches, despite differences in their parameter values.
comparison: The paper builds its experimental SMA-parameter procedure on Brooks and Cramer (1992) and Shukla et al. (1998), and discusses the chromatography transport model in relation to von Lieres and Andersson (2010).
comparison: The paper notes that SMA parameter values reported by different studies can vary with protein, pH, adsorbent, column properties, and experimental approach.
comparison: The two estimation approaches gave similar parameter order relations, although inverse estimates of characteristic charge were consistently higher and equilibrium coefficients about ten times lower.
data: Each protein and pH condition had five gradient chromatograms and a corresponding breakthrough experiment available for parameter determination.
data: The gradient and breakthrough experiments were single-component protein experiments rather than mixture separations.
equipment: All column experiments used a prepacked 1 ml HiTrap SP Sepharose FF strong cation-exchange column measuring 0.025 m long and 0.7 cm in internal diameter.
feeding: After sample loading and a further four column volumes of washing, proteins were eluted with a linear gradient from 0% to 100% high-salt buffer.
feeding: Breakthrough experiments equilibrated the column for 10 column volumes and then loaded protein isocratically until breakthrough was complete.
feeding: For gradient runs, each protein was prepared at 0.2 mM and a 20 μl sample was injected after four column volumes of equilibration.
feeding: The gradient lengths used to estimate parameters were 5, 10, 30, 60, and 120 column volumes.
fit: The inverse method produced highly precise fits for most gradient datasets at both pH conditions.
fit: The rapid-equilibrium model showed small deviations from data for the shortest, 5-column-volume gradients, which the authors attributed to neglected kinetic effects.
measurement: Online absorbance at 280 nm and 528 nm was measured in all experiments.
measurement: The inverse method fitted the mechanistic model to concentration time series derived from chromatograms measured at the column outlet.
mechanisms: The SMA model represents competition between charged modifiers and proteins for adsorbent binding sites.
mechanisms: The SMA steric correction accounts for salt ions shielded from exchange by protein-bound material.
mechanisms: The column balance represents convection, axial dispersion, and mass transfer from the mobile phase to the particle surface.
model: The chromatography model is a spatially distributed transport-dispersive model with column- and particle-level concentration balances.
model: The model solves a differential-algebraic equation system with Danckwerts boundary conditions.
model: The model tracks mobile-phase concentrations at column and particle levels and component concentrations bound to the particle surface.
operation: The column experiments were run at a flow rate of 0.5 ml/min.
operation: The running buffer was 0.02 M acetate at pH 5 or 0.02 M sodium phosphate at pH 7, and the high-salt elution buffer contained an additional 0.5 M NaCl.
parameters: Each protein is characterized by three SMA parameters under the rapid-equilibrium formulation: characteristic charge, equilibrium coefficient, and steric factor.
parameters: The inverse fit estimates the three protein-specific SMA parameters while treating other model inputs as fixed.
parameters: The paper does not state a total number of model states or equations; its numerical solution used 200 knots along the column.
prediction: Approach I predicts retention using an empirical correlation, whereas the inverse mechanistic approach can predict complete chromatograms.
sensitivity: Absolute concentration noise had nearly no influence on inverse-method SMA parameter estimates, even at the highest tested noise level.
sensitivity: Retention-time shifts affected parameter estimates more strongly than concentration noise, with the steric factor most sensitive and characteristic charge least sensitive.
sensitivity: The Monte Carlo analysis generated 10,000 chromatograms and examined concentration-noise and time-shift effects at three gradient lengths.
system: The case study models ion-exchange chromatography of ribonuclease A, cytochrome c, and lysozyme at pH 5 and pH 7.
system: The proteins were bovine-pancreas ribonuclease A, horse-heart cytochrome c, and chicken-egg-white lysozyme.
uncertainty: Multiple-start optimization indicated mean relative deviations of about 0.25% for characteristic charge estimates and about 0.5% for equilibrium-coefficient and steric-factor estimates, apart from outliers.
use: The authors recommend inverse parameter estimation for fast process development and describe the mechanistic model as useful for optimization, process control, troubleshooting, and error diagnosis.
validation: Most predicted retention volumes differed from experimental validation by less than 1 ml, including predictions for 106-column-volume gradients.
validation: The authors tested retention predictions at gradient lengths of 25, 80, and 106 column volumes for every protein at both pH conditions.
validation: The tested validation gradients were within the 5-to-120-column-volume calibration range, and the paper reports no predictions outside that range.
